title: Allevia: generous living in dense Mont'Kiara.
excerpt: Four years after covering the launch, Sean returns to a completed tower whose unit layout he calls his favourite of all time — and whose quiet dead-end street may not stay quiet.
takeaways: In Mont'Kiara the specific road matters more than the project: frontage toward the main street carries a premium because so much of life here is done on foot.
Almost 2,000 sq ft holding only three bedrooms is the point — the space goes into the living, dining, kitchen and circulation instead.
A planned road connection would trade the street's current privacy for convenience, and Sean is genuinely unsure which owners should prefer.

sections.heading: Which road you sit on
paragraphs: Sean opens with the piece of local knowledge he considers most valuable here. Within Mont'Kiara, the road a project sits on drives its pricing: frontage toward the main street carries higher returns because of the commercial support attached to it, and projects with dual frontage command a premium of their own.

The reason is walkability. Mont'Kiara is one of the few Malaysian addresses where residents genuinely live without a car, and that is much of why the expatriate community concentrates here. Live on the right block and schools, shops and cafés are all reachable on foot — so which street you face is not a detail.

Allevia sits on Jalan Kiara 4, sharing that road with a handful of neighbouring blocks. He also notes the pedestrian infrastructure as he walks it: proper separated walkways, handrails and tactile paving, which he rates as one of the things Mont'Kiara genuinely does well despite the density.

sections.heading: The dead end that may not stay one
paragraphs: The single biggest variable hanging over the project is a road. Jalan Kiara 4 currently terminates in a dead end, which means only residents of the few blocks along it use the street. Another developer is building a connection through to Jalan Kiara 3 and onward to Persiaran Dutamas.

Sean is careful not to call this an upgrade. Today, reaching the far side means driving out and making U-turns; with the connection, journeys to the international schools become direct. But the privacy of a street nobody passes through would be gone. He puts the question to viewers rather than answering it — connectivity or privacy — and says plainly that he does not know.

sections.heading: An entrance that softens the concrete
paragraphs: The arrival is where Sean's enthusiasm is most obvious. Pavers and stone replace the usual harsh concrete kerb, with landscape blended into the edges rather than fenced off from them, and planting carried over the elevated car park in the centre of the site.

The detail that surprises him most is the column treatment: concrete worked to read like draped fabric, which immediately softens the structure. Combined with the lighting design and a slate wall at the drop-off, it produces an identity he says he has not seen elsewhere in the area.

There is no step anywhere into the building — a ramp carries you from the road to the lift lobby past a checkpoint. Inside, the mail area doubles as a small seating lounge for anyone waiting, under a ceiling panel he calls genuinely dramatic.

sections.heading: Four units, four lifts
paragraphs: The floor plate is the quiet luxury of the building. Each level holds only four units, served by four lifts including a service lift, arranged two to a wing — so a resident shares their corridor with exactly one neighbour.

The corridor runs about 2.3 m wide under a 2.6 m ceiling, floored with tiles laid diagonally. Sean points out that the diagonal costs the contractor wastage at the edges but transforms how the space reads, and he approves of the door hardware chosen to resist fingerprints.

The refuse room sits off the main lobby behind partial walls with direct extract ventilation, which he considers adequate for only four units per floor. From the corridor into the unit there is again zero transition, and the entrance foyer is a generous 1.56 m.

sections.heading: Why 2,000 square feet holds three bedrooms
paragraphs: The unit filmed is a Type C1 of about 1,971 sq ft with three bedrooms, a utility room and four bathrooms. Sean flags the apparent oddity immediately — almost 2,000 sq ft and still only three bedrooms — and then explains why that is the entire point.

Entry runs down a corridor that deliberately delays the reveal before opening into a combined living and dining space roughly 6.6 m wall to wall and about 8 m from kitchen wall to balcony, under a 2.96 m ceiling with no columns or beams interrupting it. That, he says, only happens when the structural grid is designed around the layout rather than the other way round.

His conclusion is that the generous dimension goes into the in-between spaces — the living, the dining, the kitchen, the yard, the circulation — rather than into an extra bedroom. He calls it his favourite unit typology of all time, and contrasts it with the current trend of fitting three bedrooms into a fraction of the area.

sections.heading: A kitchen properly separated from the house
paragraphs: The front-of-house pantry carries the developer's own cabinetry with a matching backsplash and soft-close drawers, and at 1.71 m across Sean notes it would normally have been designed as an island with a breakfast counter.

Behind a door sits the real kitchen — about 3.67 m long and 2.27 m across, big enough that he jokes it could run commercially, with room for a second linear run of cabinets and another fridge. His one suggestion is a sliding door instead of a swing door, since the side wall allows it.

The helper's room off the kitchen has its own bathroom and is among the largest he has reviewed. The yard beyond, roughly 1.8 m square, carries the washer and dryer position, an external water point, and louvres added for privacy where it opens to the void — the place, as he puts it, where the structural untidiness gets camouflaged.

sections.heading: Bedrooms, and the view that sets the price
paragraphs: The smallest bedroom measures about 3.2 m by 5 m, which Sean observes is larger than many people's master, and looks onto a school field. It was left deliberately unfurnished by the owner so a tenant can adapt it — a tip he passes on to investors.

The master runs about 5.1 m deep by 3.6 m wall to wall, wide enough that a king bed leaves circulation space on every side along with a dressing area and wardrobe run. Its bathroom carries stone finishes, twin vanities and a bathtub, which he notes has become non-negotiable at this address, and a ramp rather than a step at the threshold so nobody stubs a toe.

The balcony is about 1.35 m deep and 5 m long with a heavy blue tint, and the outlook takes in the international school and the main commercial centre — all within walking distance. Pricing discussed in the episode ran near RM1,000 per square foot, putting a unit like this around RM1.9 to 2 million, with the furnished unit rented at about RM11,000 a month. Those figures reflect the recording date and this specific unit; the interior was also styled for rental rather than left as handed over.

sections.heading: The facilities that do not match the address
paragraphs: The deck sits between the two towers, which is itself the design move — placing the amenity where the gap between buildings is widest. The landscape architecture is expressive: cascading linear platforms, perforated screens, slanted landscape islands cutting across a rectangular canvas, and a cantilevered column-free walkway linking the towers.

The pool runs roughly 40 to 50 m with an overflow edge whose sound helps mask traffic, finished with stone rather than the usual pebble wash. A jacuzzi and children's water play are screened by planting for privacy, and the indoor badminton court is a 9 m volume with windows on all sides, air conditioning and timber flooring. The sky gym and sky lounge occupy the upper floor.

But his third concern lands here. Strip away the forms and the planting, and the list is one badminton court, a pool, a playground and a gym that was not finished at the time of filming. For a project in this price bracket he expected more, and says so — the design camouflages the facilities rather than the facilities justifying the address.
Two towers with four units per floor and step-free access throughout.
A 1,971 sq ft unit with only three bedrooms, renting fully furnished for RM11,000.
Density, a planned road link and basic facilities are the concerns.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: Allevia has two square towers with just four units per floor, served by four lifts, and a level, step-free route from the drop-off to the front door. The 1,971 sq ft Type C1 has only three bedrooms plus a utility room, so the space goes to the shared rooms: a column-free living and dining area of about 7 by 8 metres under a 3-metre ceiling, a separate wet kitchen beside the pantry, and a large helper's room.
Units were changing hands at around RM1,000 psf, about RM1.9 million to RM2 million.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: It is on Jalan Mont Kiara 4, for now a dead end used only by residents of a few blocks, with a side gate to Jalan Mont Kiara 3. Mont Kiara International School, Garden International School and the 163 and Arcoris shops and offices are within walking distance.

sections.heading: Rent and returns
paragraphs: This fully furnished unit rents for RM11,000 a month, and a one-bedroom at 163 for about RM6,000. The demand comes from expatriates on three- to five-year postings, who would rather rent somewhere comfortable than buy. At about RM2 million, Sean puts the instalment at RM8,000 to RM10,000, so the rent covers it.
An investor's tip from the unit: the owner left the smallest bedroom empty, so a tenant can make it a study, nursery or hobby room without furniture having to be moved out.

pros: Mont'Kiara's international schools, mature amenities and walkability let residents live without a car, which is why the expatriate community concentrates here and why short-stay tenants pay strong rents.

The towers are placed as far apart as the site allows and oriented to protect views, and the architecture — fabric-like columns, considered lighting, zero step-up throughout, expressive landscape islands — is unlike anything else on the street.

The unit typology is his all-time favourite: a horizontal layout with living and dining together and bedrooms split to the sides, where nearly 2,000 sq ft buys generous in-between space rather than a fourth bedroom.
cons: Mont'Kiara keeps absorbing new supply, with more plots along the neighbouring road still to be developed — daunting for anyone not already familiar with how the location performs.
The planned Jalan Kiara 3 to 4 connection would make school runs direct but end the privacy of a dead-end street, and he is genuinely undecided about which owners should want.
The facilities are minimal for this price bracket — one badminton court, a pool, a playground and an incomplete gym — well decorated, but thin compared with what similar money buys elsewhere.

sections.closing: Allevia's argument is made inside the unit, not on the facilities deck. Whether that is enough depends on how much a buyer values the address, the walkability and a layout that spends its square footage on living space — and on which way the road at the end of the street eventually goes.
sections.sourceNote: Based on Sean's full public English captions and his published YouTube episode notes. Measurements, unit size, asking prices and rents are as discussed in the video and reflect the recording date; the unit filmed had been furnished for rental rather than left as handed over. The 3 on 3 section paraphrases the three things Sean says he likes and the three he has concerns about, presented near the end of the episode.

Mont Kiara itself: mature amenities, walkable without a car, and more international schools than anywhere else, which keeps expatriate demand and rents high. This unit fetches RM11,000; a one-bedroom at 163 about RM6,000.
The design: towers spaced apart and angled for views, speed ramps in the car park, fabric-textured concrete, step-free access and an inventive landscaped deck.
Sean's favourite layout: nearly 2,000 sq ft with only three bedrooms, so the living, dining, kitchen and in-between spaces are generous, with big windows throughout.

cons: Density and new supply, with more plots still to be built along Jalan Mont Kiara 3; the numbers still work, as an instalment of about RM8,000 to RM10,000 is covered by rent of RM10,000 to RM11,000.
A planned link from Jalan Mont Kiara 4 to Jalan Mont Kiara 3 would make trips such as the school run easier, but end the privacy of the dead end.
Basic facilities for about RM1,000 psf: one badminton court, a pool, a playground, an unfinished gym and an unremarkable rooftop, dressed up by good design.
closing: For walkable Mont Kiara living with generous space, Allevia delivers; just don't buy it for the facilities.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this October 2025 episode. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three concerns he names, in his order, at the end of the video. An owner let Sean view the unit; prices and rents are as he quoted them.
